name: OK Soda
tierWhy: Coca-Cola said in September 1995 that it would phase the drink out of its test markets; its US registration of the OK soft drink trademark was cancelled in 2003, and we found no drink sold under the name since.[^9][^11]

title: OK Soda (1994–1995): post-mortem · Spectre Brands
description: Coca-Cola built a soda for Generation X out of grey cans, chain letters and a telephone hotline, tested it in nine cities and dropped it after about a million cases. A sourced post-mortem from the press of 1994–1995, Coca-Cola’s filings and trademark records.

card.blurb: Coca-Cola’s soda for people who distrusted advertising came in grey cans with a hotline and a manifesto. The hotline took more than a million calls. The drink sold about a million cases and never left its test markets.

stat.label: cases sold in its test markets before Coca-Cola phased it out

hero.dates: Introduced Apr 20, 1994. On sale in test markets from May 1994. Phase-out reported Sep 13, 1995.
hero.standfirst: The slogan was “Things are going to be OK.” For the people who called the hotline, perhaps. For the soda, no.
hero.deck: OK Soda was a reddish-brown, fruity soft drink that Coca-Cola aimed at 12- to 25-year-olds in 1994, with drab cans drawn by alternative cartoonists, chain letters in the mail and a toll-free number that played back callers’ complaints. Coca-Cola hoped it would become a mainstream brand, and the press reported a target of 3 to 4% of the market. It was sold in eight or nine US cities, depending on the source, and was withdrawn after a little more than a million cases. Coca-Cola’s SEC filings mention it once, in a list of products, so this post-mortem is built mostly from the newspapers and magazines of the time. It has fewer numbers than most pages on this site, and says where the record stops.
hero.artCaption: Original illustration of a soda can with a blank face. Not an official asset; the face, the label and the lettering are our own drawing, not the artwork on the real cans.

findings.title: The brand came before the drink.
findings.text: Advertising Age reported five days after the announcement that Coca-Cola would bring to market “a new brand that’s admittedly not fully formed.”[^5] The Believer later reported that the ads were grey partly because the color of the liquid had not been decided.[^13]

findings.title: The campaign was the part that worked.
findings.text: Coca-Cola said the hotline had taken more than a million calls within about four months, from a product on sale in a handful of cities.[^8]

findings.title: The taste was the part that did not.
findings.text: The first four people a Washington Post reporter asked in Minneapolis each compared it to a “suicide,” every soda fountain flavor in one cup. A nine-store supermarket chain there sold at most ten 12-packs a week.[^8]

findings.title: It was judged as a mainstream brand.
findings.text: The target was 3 to 4% of the market, about the size of Mountain Dew.[^8][^6] What it delivered was a little over a million cases, which a spokesman said was not “the type of profitable volume we needed.”[^9]

findings.title: Nobody has brought it back.
findings.text: The trademark registration issued in 1997, after the drink was gone, and was cancelled in 2003.[^11] We found no re-release.
